## Symmetric / Skew-Symmetric Decomposition of $Lu = -\mu\Delta u + \mathbf{b}\cdot\nabla u$

### Setup

We work on $L^2(\Omega)$ with the inner product $(u,v)=\int_\Omega u\,v\,dx$, and assume functions vanish on $\partial\Omega$ (or are periodic) so that all boundary integrals vanish. We seek the decomposition

$$L = L_s + L_a, \qquad L_s^* = L_s \;\text{(self-adjoint)},\quad L_a^* = -L_a \;\text{(skew-adjoint)},$$

given by $L_s = \tfrac12(L+L^*)$, $L_a = \tfrac12(L-L^*)$.

### Computing the adjoint $L^*$

**Diffusion term.** With $\mu$ constant, $-\mu\Delta$ is self-adjoint: integrating by parts twice gives $(-\mu\Delta)^* = -\mu\Delta$.

**Transport term.** For each component, integrating by parts once:

$$\int_\Omega (b_j\,\partial_j u)\,v\,dx = -\int_\Omega u\,\partial_j(b_j v)\,dx = -\int_\Omega u\,(\partial_j b_j)\,v\,dx - \int_\Omega u\,b_j\,\partial_j v\,dx.$$

Summing over $j$:

$$(\mathbf{b}\cdot\nabla)^* v = -\mathbf{b}\cdot\nabla v - (\nabla\cdot\mathbf{b})\,v.$$

Therefore

$$\boxed{L^* = -\mu\Delta - \mathbf{b}\cdot\nabla - \nabla\cdot\mathbf{b}.}$$

### Symmetric part

$$L_s = \tfrac12(L+L^*) = \tfrac12\bigl[(-\mu\Delta + \mathbf{b}\cdot\nabla) + (-\mu\Delta - \mathbf{b}\cdot\nabla - \nabla\cdot\mathbf{b})\bigr]$$

$$\boxed{L_s u = -\mu\,\Delta u - \tfrac12(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{b})\,u.}$$

This is self-adjoint: $-\mu\Delta$ is self-adjoint, and $-\tfrac12(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{b})$ is a (real) multiplication operator, hence self-adjoint.

### Skew-symmetric part

$$L_a = \tfrac12(L-L^*) = \tfrac12\bigl[(-\mu\Delta + \mathbf{b}\cdot\nabla) - (-\mu\Delta - \mathbf{b}\cdot\nabla - \nabla\cdot\mathbf{b})\bigr]$$

$$\boxed{L_a u = \mathbf{b}\cdot\nabla u + \tfrac12(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{b})\,u.}$$

**Verification of skew-symmetry.** Using $(\mathbf{b}\cdot\nabla)^* = -\mathbf{b}\cdot\nabla - \nabla\cdot\mathbf{b}$ and the fact that $\tfrac12(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{b})$ is self-adjoint (multiplication):

$$L_a^* = (-\mathbf{b}\cdot\nabla - \nabla\cdot\mathbf{b}) + \tfrac12(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{b}) = -\mathbf{b}\cdot\nabla - \tfrac12(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{b}) = -L_a.\quad\checkmark$$

### Equivalent divergence (conservative) form of $L_a$

Using $\nabla\cdot(\mathbf{b}\,u) = (\nabla\cdot\mathbf{b})\,u + \mathbf{b}\cdot\nabla u$, we may rewrite

$$L_a u = \tfrac12\bigl[\mathbf{b}\cdot\nabla u + \nabla\cdot(\mathbf{b}\,u)\bigr],$$

i.e. $L_a$ is the **average** of the non-divergence and divergence forms of the transport operator. This makes skew-adjointness immediate: for any $u,v$ vanishing on the boundary,

$$(L_a u, v) = \tfrac12\int_\Omega\bigl[\mathbf{b}\cdot\nabla u\,v + \nabla\cdot(\mathbf{b}u)\,v\bigr]dx = \tfrac12\int_\Omega\bigl[\mathbf{b}\cdot\nabla u\,v - \mathbf{b}u\cdot\nabla v\bigr]dx,$$

which is antisymmetric in $u,v$, so $(L_a u,v) = -(u, L_a v)$.

### Consistency check

$$L_s + L_a = \bigl[-\mu\Delta - \tfrac12\nabla\cdot\mathbf{b}\bigr] + \bigl[\mathbf{b}\cdot\nabla + \tfrac12\nabla\cdot\mathbf{b}\bigr] = -\mu\Delta + \mathbf{b}\cdot\nabla = L.\quad\checkmark$$

### Summary

$$Lu = \underbrace{-\mu\,\Delta u - \tfrac12(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{b})\,u}_{L_s\;\text{(symmetric)}} \;+\; \underbrace{\mathbf{b}\cdot\nabla u + \tfrac12(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{b})\,u}_{L_a\;\text{(skew-symmetric)}}.$$

Equivalently, $L_a u = \tfrac12\bigl[\mathbf{b}\cdot\nabla u + \nabla\cdot(\mathbf{b}\,u)\bigr]$.
